title: The SS Waratah: How Did a Brand-New Liner Vanish With 211 People?
case_title: The Loss of the SS Waratah
case_meta: Off the Wild Coast, South Africa · July 1909
subject: waratah
description:
What do you think happened to the Waratah after her last signal? 👇

In July 1909 the Blue Anchor Line's new flagship left Durban for Cape Town with 211 people aboard and was never seen again. No lifeboat, no wreckage and no survivor was ever confirmed. This case file follows her last signals, the months of searching, the 1910 Board of Trade inquiry where a passenger who left the ship described his dreams, and the decades-long hunt for the wreck off South Africa's coast.

Sources: State Library of South Australia, "Australia's Titanic: the sinking of SS Waratah"; UK Parliament, Hansard, 5 July 1910; Journal of Maritime Archaeology (2025); Taranaki Daily News, 19 December 1910, and Horowhenua Chronicle, 13 February 1911 (Papers Past); Mail & Guardian, 19 April 2004; South African History Online; Wikipedia, "SS Waratah" and its references.

scenes.text: Claude Sawyer had paid for a passage all the way to Cape Town. When the ship docked in Durban, he walked down the gangway with his luggage and did not come back.
He sent his wife a short cable. It read: "Thought Waratah top-heavy, landed Durban." He gave the crew no reason for leaving.
On the evening of the 26th of July, the Waratah sailed on without him. She was less than a year old, the flagship of her line, with 211 people aboard.
She was due in Cape Town three days later. She never arrived. No lifeboat, no body and no wreckage proven to be hers was ever found.
Sawyer would later tell an official inquiry what had made him leave. Part of his answer was about the ship's roll. Part of it was about a dream.
The Waratah was launched on the 12th of September 1908 at the Barclay, Curle yard on the River Clyde in Glasgow. She was built for the Blue Anchor Line of London.
Blue Anchor carried emigrants and cargo between Britain and Australia by way of South Africa. The new ship was meant to lead its fleet.
She measured about 465 feet and more than nine thousand tons. She had cabins for first-class travellers and room below decks for hundreds of emigrants.
Her master was Captain Ilbery, a long-serving Blue Anchor commander with decades at sea, who had previously sailed the company's older ship Geelong.
The Waratah left London on her maiden voyage on the 5th of November 1908. After the round trip, Ilbery was not entirely happy with how she behaved.
At the later inquiry, the owners said he had been convinced that her stability was less than that of the Geelong. The builders insisted the two ships were equal.
Another witness remembered Ilbery calling her "a very handy ship" after that first trip. Whatever he really thought, he took her out again.
On the second voyage she reached Australia safely and loaded cargo, including lead concentrate. On the 7th of July 1909 she left Adelaide for London, by way of Durban.
After a stop in Durban, she put to sea again around a quarter past eight in the evening of the 26th of July, carrying 92 passengers and 119 crew.
Early the next morning, off the coast of what is now the Eastern Cape, she came up behind a slower cargo steamer, the Clan MacIntyre.
The two ships exchanged lamp signals, each giving its name and destination. Then the Waratah pulled ahead. By about half past nine, she was over the horizon.
That was the last time anyone positively identified her. The weather was already turning. Within a day, a violent gale was blowing along that coast.
That evening the crew of another steamer, the Harlow, saw smoke and the lights of a ship far astern. Then came two bright flashes, and the lights were gone.
According to the Harlow's crew, the mate took the flashes for bush fires on the shore, and the captain did not record them in the log.
Later that night, a Union-Castle liner, the Guelph, exchanged lamp signals with an unknown ship. Her signaller could read only three letters: T, A, H.
Not everyone agreed that all of these lights belonged to the Waratah. Somewhere between Durban and Cape Town, she was simply gone.
When she failed to reach Cape Town on the 29th of July, nobody panicked at first. A breakdown seemed likely. A ship that size might be drifting, waiting for help.
The Royal Navy sent the cruisers Pandora and Forte to sweep the coast, and later HMS Hermes. Day after day, their lookouts saw only open water.
False hope came quickly. A cable reported a Blue Anchor ship slowly making for Durban. It was read out in the Australian parliament. It was not the Waratah.
Weeks passed without a single confirmed sighting. No lifebelt, deck chair or empty boat was ever shown to have come from her.
The Blue Anchor Line chartered the steamer Sabine to follow the ship's likely drift path. She covered about fourteen thousand miles of ocean.
By the end of the year, almost no one expected to find her afloat. The families still hoped, and they organised one more voyage of their own.
Their chartered ship, the Wakefield, set out early in 1910. She spent months at sea and sailed about fifteen thousand miles. She found nothing at all.
The Board of Trade ordered a formal investigation in February 1910. It sat that December at Caxton Hall in London.
Expert witnesses said the Waratah had been properly designed and well built. A chief surveyor for Lloyd's called her a strong ship.
Then came witnesses who had sailed in her. A steward said he left because he disliked the rolling. A seaman said plainly that she was top-heavy.
Claude Sawyer said she rolled heavily and recovered slowly. He described a long, jerky roll that made him uneasy, and said some passengers had been hurt.
He told the court he had raised a roll of 45 degrees with one of the officers. The answer, he said, was: "The builders have seen to the roll; it is all right."
Finally, he told the court about his dreams. Before Durban, he had dreamed three times of a man in strange clothes, holding a long sword.
After he went ashore, he said, he dreamed of the ship itself. A big roller came over her bow, she rolled onto her starboard side, and disappeared.
Sawyer himself said the dreams had grown out of his bad impressions of the ship. The question for the court was whether those impressions were right.
The court never settled that question. It could not say what had happened, and it put no blame on the Blue Anchor Line.
The most common explanation is the storm. If the Waratah was as tender as some witnesses believed, a heavy sea could have rolled her over before anyone reached a lifeboat.
Some researchers point to cargo. Hundreds of tons of lead concentrate could have shifted in a violent roll, leaving her listing and unable to recover.
Others think of freak waves. That coast lies along the Agulhas Current, where storm swells running against the current can build into unusually steep, high walls of water.
Some linked the Harlow's two flashes to an explosion in a coal bunker. There is no proof that the lights the Harlow saw belonged to the Waratah.
Every theory has the same problem. Without a wreck, none of them can be tested, and the ship has never been found.
Clues kept surfacing for decades. In 1929, Edward Joe Conquer, a former Cape Mounted Rifleman, said that in July 1909 he had seen a steamer roll heavily and vanish near the Xora River.
In 1962, a pilot named Bill Elston said he had flown over the same coast and seen the shape of a ship beneath the water, "listing considerably to starboard".
The South African researcher Emlyn Brown spent more than twenty years searching that stretch of sea. In 1999 he announced that sonar had found her.
Divers reached the wreck in 2001. It was the Nailsea Meadow, a cargo ship sunk by a German U-boat during the Second World War.
In 2004, after one more expedition, Brown stopped. "I've exhausted all the options," he said. "I now have no idea where to look."

scenes.text: The Blue Anchor Line did not survive the loss. Passengers stayed away, and within a year its remaining ships had been sold to P&O.
In Higher Cemetery, in the English city of Exeter, a memorial carries the name of Thomas Newman, one of those lost. Families like his never had a wreck to visit.
More than a century later, the Waratah has still not been found. The clearest warning on record came from the passenger who thought she was top-heavy and walked ashore in Durban.
